triage.name: Delirium
triage.reason: Acute confusional state with fluctuating course; core hospital diagnosis reached by history, exam and workup for toxic, metabolic and infectious causes.

demographics: Most common in hospitalized older adults, especially those with pre-existing cognitive impairment
Occurs at any age in the setting of severe illness, surgery, or drug or alcohol withdrawal
More common in nursing home residents and patients in intensive care

risk_factors.text: Pre-existing dementia or mild cognitive impairment
Hospitalization, especially ICU admission or recent surgery
Infection such as urinary tract infection or pneumonia
Use of psychoactive medications (sedatives, opioids, anticholinergics)
Alcohol or drug intoxication or withdrawal
Metabolic derangement, dehydration, or electrolyte imbalance
Severe pain, sleep deprivation, or use of physical restraints
Multiple chronic illnesses or organ failure

comorbidities: Chronic kidney disease or liver failure
Prior stroke or other structural brain lesion
social_history: Lives in a nursing home or assisted living facility
Recent change in living situation or loss of a spouse
exposures: Recent infection in the community or hospital

chief_complaints.text: I don't know where I am or what day it is
My family says I've been confused and not making sense since yesterday
I keep seeing things that aren't there
I can't stay awake or focus on what people are saying

hpi.onset: Sudden, over hours to a few days
hpi.duration: Hours to days at presentation; may fluctuate and persist for weeks if the cause is not treated
hpi.progression: Symptoms come and go during the day, often worse at night; level of alertness and orientation change from hour to hour
hpi.quality: Fluctuating confusion with difficulty paying attention and organizing thoughts
hpi.severity: Moderate to severe; interferes with conversation, self-care and safety
hpi.timing: Worse in the evening and at night; may be more alert and oriented in the morning

associated_symptoms.text: Trouble concentrating or following a conversation
Disorientation to time, place or person
Disrupted sleep-wake cycle with daytime sleepiness and nighttime wakefulness
Tremor, sweating or rapid heartbeat in withdrawal states

pertinent_negatives: Gradual memory decline over months to years before this episode
Focal weakness, numbness or difficulty speaking
New severe headache or head trauma
Loss of consciousness or seizure before the confusion started
Fever with stiff neck or rash
Intentional overdose or recent suicide attempt

positives.text: Feeling tired or sleepy during the day
Fever or chills if infection is the cause

argues_against: Head trauma with loss of consciousness

negatives: Long-standing depressed mood before this episode
argues_against: Primary psychiatric disorder with stable course

positives.text: Burning with urination or frequent urination
Low blood pressure or dizziness on standing
Cough or shortness of breath if pneumonia is the cause

atypical.how_it_differs: Hypoactive delirium is most common in this group and is often mistaken for depression, fatigue or dementia; patients may be quiet, withdrawn and sleepy rather than agitated.
missing_classic_features: Obvious confusion reported by the patient

atypical.how_it_differs: Children may present with irritability, inconsolable crying, refusal to eat, or regression of behavior rather than clear disorientation; they may not report hallucinations.
Infants show poor feeding, lethargy or inconsolable fussiness; the diagnosis is usually made when an underlying illness or medication effect is identified.
missing_classic_features: Fluctuating attention noted by the patient

atypical.how_it_differs: Infection may be the trigger with minimal or no fever, so delirium can be the only sign of a serious infection.
Accumulation of medications and metabolic waste can cause or worsen delirium; symptoms may persist until dialysis or dose adjustment.
missing_classic_features: Rapid improvement after treating a single obvious cause

atypical.how_it_differs: Hepatic encephalopathy can present with fluctuating confusion, sleep inversion and asterixis; it may be mistaken for primary delirium from another cause.
Delirium in pregnancy is uncommon and usually signals a severe underlying condition such as eclampsia, sepsis, or a medication reaction; presentation may be dominated by obstetric symptoms.

general.mild: Awake but easily distracted; may appear tired or mildly restless; conversation drifts off topic
general.moderate: Clearly inattentive and disoriented; either drowsy and withdrawn or restless and picking at lines or clothing
general.severe: Markedly confused; may be agitated and attempting to climb out of bed, or somnolent and only briefly rousable
general.critical: Fluctuating between agitation and unresponsiveness; may be combative or barely arousable; autonomic overactivity if withdrawal or severe systemic illness

findings.maneuver: Ask the patient to recite the months backward or spell 'world' backward
findings.finding: Cannot sustain attention; makes errors or loses track of the task

findings.maneuver: Ask the patient their name, where they are, and the date or day of the week
findings.finding: Disoriented to time, place, or person

findings.maneuver: Observe and re-examine the patient over minutes to hours, or compare with nursing reports from earlier in the day
findings.finding: Level of alertness and orientation changes during the day, often worse at night

findings.maneuver: Observe the patient's level of arousal and response to voice or touch
findings.finding: Reduced or fluctuating level of consciousness (drowsy, hypervigilant, or difficult to arouse)

findings.maneuver: Listen to the patient's spontaneous speech and ask open-ended questions
findings.finding: Rambling, tangential, or incoherent speech

findings.maneuver: Give three words and ask the patient to repeat them after a few minutes
findings.finding: Impaired short-term recall

findings.maneuver: Ask whether the patient sees or hears things others do not
findings.finding: Visual or auditory hallucinations, often frightening

findings.maneuver: Ask about suspicious or fixed false beliefs
findings.finding: Paranoid or persecutory delusions
Restlessness, pulling at lines or clothing, attempting to get out of bed

findings.maneuver: Observe the patient's spontaneous activity and interaction
findings.finding: Withdrawn, sleepy, or slow to respond; easily mistaken for depression or fatigue

findings.maneuver: Ask the patient to extend both arms with wrists dorsiflexed and observe for a few seconds
findings.finding: Brief, irregular flapping of the hands (suggests hepatic encephalopathy or metabolic cause)

findings.maneuver: Observe the outstretched hands and ask the patient to hold a steady posture
findings.finding: Postural or intention tremor (suggests alcohol or sedative withdrawal, or medication effect)

findings.maneuver: Test strength, sensation, and cranial nerves, and ask the patient to smile and raise both arms
findings.finding: No focal weakness, sensory loss, or facial droop

findings.maneuver: Flex the neck and check for resistance or pain
findings.finding: No neck stiffness or meningismus

findings.maneuver: Inspect the scalp and ask about recent falls or head injury
findings.finding: No scalp laceration, hematoma, or signs of trauma

findings.maneuver: Inspect the skin, including the back and pressure areas
findings.finding: No petechial or purpuric rash

findings.maneuver: Auscultate the lungs and inspect for a source of infection
findings.finding: No focal crackles or consolidation to suggest pneumonia

labs.caveat: Hyponatremia is a common reversible cause; correct slowly to avoid osmotic demyelination.
Hypernatremia from dehydration or poor access to water, especially in nursing home residents.
Hypercalcemia causes confusion and lethargy; check ionized calcium if albumin is low.
Hypoglycemia is a rapidly reversible cause; check a bedside glucose immediately in any confused patient.
Severe hyperglycemia suggests diabetic ketoacidosis or hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state.
Uremia from renal failure or dehydration contributes to encephalopathy.
Also guides safe dosing of sedatives and antipsychotics.
Elevated in hepatic encephalopathy; a normal level does not exclude it.
Severe hypothyroidism can present with confusion and hypothermia; hyperthyroidism can mimic agitated delirium.
Leukocytosis supports infection as the trigger; a normal count does not exclude it, especially in older adults.
Urinary tract infection is a frequent precipitant; asymptomatic bacteriuria is common in older adults and may not be the true cause.
Elevation suggests sepsis, hypoperfusion, or alcohol-related thiamine deficiency.
Only when meningitis or encephalitis is suspected; a normal CSF cell count does not exclude early infection.
Low CSF glucose relative to serum suggests bacterial meningitis.

findings.finding: Sinus tachycardia from infection, dehydration, pain, or alcohol or sedative withdrawal
Atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response, a common precipitant of delirium in older adults
Prolonged QTc from electrolyte derangement or QT-prolonging medications such as haloperidol
ST depression or elevation suggesting myocardial ischemia or infarction as the trigger
Peaked T waves with widened QRS in hyperkalemia, or flattened T waves and U waves in hypokalemia

imaging.preferred_when: New focal neurologic deficit, head trauma, anticoagulation, or no clear cause identified

findings.text: Cerebral atrophy consistent with underlying dementia

imaging.study: MRI brain with and without IV contrast
imaging.preferred_when: Suspected encephalitis, abscess, or when CT is nondiagnostic

findings.text: Temporal lobe signal abnormality suggesting herpes simplex encephalitis
Ring-enhancing lesion suggesting abscess or tumor
Diffuse white matter changes consistent with small vessel disease

imaging.preferred_when: Fever, cough, hypoxia, or suspected pneumonia

findings.text: Lobar consolidation or infiltrate suggesting pneumonia

imaging.study: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast
imaging.preferred_when: Abdominal pain, fever without a source, or suspected intra-abdominal infection
Suspected nonconvulsive status epilepticus or unexplained persistent unresponsiveness

findings.text: Diffuse slowing consistent with metabolic encephalopathy
Triphasic waves suggesting hepatic or metabolic encephalopathy
Epileptiform discharges or nonconvulsive status epilepticus

initial.why: Detects hyponatremia, hypercalcemia, uremia, and acid-base disturbance, all common reversible causes
Looks for infection or anemia as a trigger
Bedside glucose is mandatory; hypoglycemia is immediately reversible
Urinary tract infection is a frequent precipitant in older adults
Thyroid dysfunction can present with confusion
Deficiency is a reversible cause of cognitive impairment
Detects arrhythmia, ischemia, or QT prolongation relevant to treatment

initial.only_if: fever, cough, hypoxia, or suspected pneumonia
new focal deficit, head trauma, anticoagulation, or no cause found
fever with headache, neck stiffness, or rash, or unexplained delirium with no other source

confirmatory.why: Bedside structured assessment confirming acute onset, fluctuating course, inattention, and disorganized thinking or altered consciousness

supporting.why: Supports hepatic encephalopathy when liver disease is suspected
Adds evidence of infection or inflammation
Supports bacterial infection when the source is unclear
Hypomagnesemia can cause confusion and arrhythmia
Low phosphate contributes to weakness and confusion
Ionized calcium when albumin is low or calcium is borderline
Adrenal insufficiency can present with confusion and hypotension
Pregnancy alters the differential and management
supporting.only_if: patient is a woman of childbearing age

supporting.test: MRI brain with and without IV contrast
supporting.only_if: suspected encephalitis, abscess, or nondiagnostic CT
persistent unexplained unresponsiveness or suspected seizures

supporting.test: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast
supporting.only_if: abdominal pain or fever without a source

not_indicated.why: Not routine when the cause is clearly metabolic or infectious and there is no focal deficit or trauma

not_indicated.test: MRI brain with and without IV contrast
not_indicated.why: Not first-line; reserved for suspected encephalitis or abscess

not_indicated.test: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast
not_indicated.why: Not routine without abdominal findings or fever of unknown source
Not routine without signs of CNS infection
Not routine unless seizures or nonconvulsive status are suspected
Not routine without respiratory symptoms or fever
Not needed in men or women who cannot be pregnant

decision_points: Check bedside glucose immediately in any patient with acute confusion
Review the full medication list and stop or reduce deliriogenic drugs
Look for and treat infection, dehydration, and electrolyte disturbance before attributing symptoms to dementia or a psychiatric disorder
Image the brain when there is focal deficit, trauma, anticoagulation, or no identified cause
Perform lumbar puncture when CNS infection is suspected, after imaging if there are focal signs or immunocompromise
Use the CAM or similar structured tool to confirm the diagnosis at the bedside

criteria.name: Confusion Assessment Method (CAM)
criteria.summary: Bedside tool that identifies delirium when there is an acute change with fluctuating course plus inattention, and either disorganized thinking or an altered level of consciousness.

differential.name: Dementia
differential.why_considered: Both cause confusion and disorientation in older adults, and the two frequently coexist; dementia is the strongest risk factor for delirium.

history: Gradual decline in memory and function over months to years
Stable, slowly progressive course rather than hour-to-hour fluctuation
Attention relatively preserved until late stages
No acute medical trigger
exam: Alert and attentive at baseline; can engage in conversation
labs: Workup for reversible causes is unrevealing
B12, TSH and metabolic panel normal or showing chronic stable abnormalities
imaging: CT or MRI shows cerebral atrophy or chronic vascular changes without an acute lesion

differential.name: Depression
differential.why_considered: Hypoactive delirium is easily mistaken for depression because both cause withdrawal, reduced interaction, poor appetite and slowed responses.

history: Weeks to months of low mood, anhedonia and hopelessness
No acute onset or fluctuation during the day
Intact attention and orientation
No acute medical illness or new medication
labs: Metabolic, infectious and toxic workup unrevealing

differential.name: Psychosis (primary psychiatric disorder)
differential.why_considered: Hyperactive delirium with hallucinations, delusions and agitation can resemble a primary psychotic disorder such as schizophrenia.

history: Long-standing or recurrent psychotic symptoms before this episode
Clear sensorium and orientation between episodes
No acute medical trigger
Auditory hallucinations more typical than visual

differential.name: Nonconvulsive status epilepticus
differential.why_considered: Can present with fluctuating confusion, altered awareness and subtle motor signs, mimicking delirium.
differential.trigger: Persistent unexplained altered mental status that does not improve after correcting obvious causes

history: Known epilepsy or prior seizures
Prolonged unresponsiveness or staring spells
Subtle twitching of face or limbs
exam: Subtle myoclonic jerks or eye deviation
imaging: EEG shows continuous or repetitive epileptiform discharges

differential.name: Meningitis or encephalitis
differential.why_considered: CNS infection can present with acute confusion, fever and altered consciousness, and is a life-threatening cause of delirium.
differential.trigger: Fever with headache, neck stiffness, rash, or delirium without another source

history: Fever, headache, photophobia
Neck stiffness
Recent viral illness or rash
exam: Meningismus, positive Kernig or Brudzinski sign
labs: CSF pleocytosis, elevated protein, low glucose
imaging: MRI temporal lobe signal abnormality in herpes simplex encephalitis
CT may be normal or show complications

differential.name: Alcohol or sedative withdrawal (delirium tremens)
differential.why_considered: Withdrawal causes agitation, confusion, hallucinations and autonomic overactivity, closely resembling hyperactive delirium.
differential.trigger: Recent cessation or reduction of heavy alcohol or sedative use with tremor, sweating and tachycardia

history: Heavy chronic alcohol or benzodiazepine use
Last drink or dose 1–5 days ago
Prior withdrawal seizures

differential.name: Hepatic encephalopathy
differential.why_considered: Fluctuating confusion, sleep inversion and asterixis can mimic delirium and often coexist with it.

history: Known cirrhosis or liver disease
Precipitant such as GI bleed, infection, constipation or dehydration
Sleep-wake inversion

differential.name: Hypoglycemia
differential.why_considered: Low blood glucose causes acute confusion, agitation and altered consciousness that resolves rapidly with treatment.
differential.trigger: Any patient with acute confusion; check bedside glucose immediately

history: Diabetes treated with insulin or sulfonylureas
Missed meal, increased activity, or recent dose change
Diaphoresis, palpitations, hunger
labs: Low bedside glucose that corrects with dextrose

severity.mild: Early or subtle: mild inattention and disorientation that fluctuate; patient can still converse and follow simple commands; often recognized only by family or nursing staff.
severity.moderate: Established: clear inattention, disorientation and either agitation or withdrawal; interferes with self-care and safety; requires close supervision.
severity.severe: Marked confusion with agitation or somnolence; may attempt to climb out of bed or be difficult to arouse; autonomic instability if withdrawal or severe systemic illness; high risk of falls and injury.
severity.critical: Life-threatening: fluctuating between combativeness and unresponsiveness; autonomic overactivity with fever, tachycardia and hypertension in severe withdrawal; or delirium as the presenting sign of sepsis, hypoxia or intracranial catastrophe.

red_flags.finding: Fever with neck stiffness, headache or rash
red_flags.meaning: Possible meningitis or encephalitis; needs urgent lumbar puncture and empiric treatment

red_flags.finding: New focal neurologic deficit, seizure or head trauma
red_flags.meaning: Structural brain lesion such as stroke, hemorrhage or subdural hematoma; needs urgent imaging

red_flags.finding: Hypotension, tachycardia, tachypnea or elevated lactate
red_flags.meaning: Sepsis or hypoperfusion; delirium may be the only early sign in older adults

red_flags.finding: Low oxygen saturation or respiratory distress
red_flags.meaning: Hypoxia or pneumonia as the trigger; needs immediate oxygen and workup

red_flags.finding: Severe agitation with autonomic overactivity after alcohol or sedative cessation
red_flags.meaning: Delirium tremens; risk of seizures, arrhythmia and death without treatment

red_flags.finding: Persistent unexplained unresponsiveness despite correcting obvious causes
red_flags.meaning: Possible nonconvulsive status epilepticus; needs EEG

complications.name: Falls and fractures
clues: Agitation or attempts to climb out of bed

complications.name: Functional decline and loss of independence
clues: New dependence in activities of daily living

special_populations.differences: Hypoactive delirium is most common and is often mistaken for depression, fatigue or dementia; symptoms may be subtle and recognized only by family or nursing staff. Higher risk of falls, functional decline and mortality.

May present with irritability, inconsolable crying, refusal to eat or behavioral regression rather than clear disorientation; they may not report hallucinations. Diagnosis relies on observation and identifying an underlying cause.
Show poor feeding, lethargy or inconsolable fussiness; the diagnosis is usually made when an underlying illness or medication effect is identified.
Delirium in pregnancy is uncommon and usually signals a severe underlying condition such as eclampsia, sepsis or a medication reaction; presentation may be dominated by obstetric symptoms.
Infection may be the trigger with minimal or no fever, so delirium can be the only sign of a serious infection; a lower threshold for imaging and lumbar puncture is warranted.
Accumulation of medications and metabolic waste can cause or worsen delirium; symptoms may persist until dialysis or dose adjustment. Careful dosing of sedatives and antipsychotics is essential.

Hepatic encephalopathy can present with fluctuating confusion, sleep inversion and asterixis; it may be mistaken for primary delirium from another cause. Ammonia levels and clinical response to lactulose help distinguish.

key_questions.question: When did the confusion start, and has it changed since then?
key_questions.looking_for: Sudden onset over hours to a few days with fluctuation during the day; a gradual decline over months points to dementia instead

key_questions.question: Is the patient more confused at certain times of day, especially at night?
key_questions.looking_for: Worse in the evening and at night with clearer periods in the morning; fluctuation is a core feature

key_questions.question: Can the patient hold attention, follow a conversation, or does their mind wander?
key_questions.looking_for: Inattention and difficulty tracking conversation; attention is the key deficit in delirium

key_questions.question: Has the patient been sleepy and withdrawn, or restless and agitated?
key_questions.looking_for: Hypoactive, hyperactive or mixed pattern; hypoactive is most common in older adults and easily missed

key_questions.question: Any fever, cough, burning with urination, or other signs of infection?
key_questions.looking_for: Urinary tract infection, pneumonia or another infection as the trigger

key_questions.question: Has the patient had any falls, head injury, or new weakness, numbness or trouble speaking?
key_questions.looking_for: Head trauma, subdural hematoma, or stroke; focal deficits or trauma require urgent imaging

key_questions.question: What medications has the patient started, stopped or had dose changes on recently?
key_questions.looking_for: Sedatives, opioids, anticholinergics, steroids or other deliriogenic drugs; also withdrawal from stopped medications

key_questions.question: How much alcohol or sedative medication does the patient use, and when was the last drink or dose?
key_questions.looking_for: Heavy chronic use with recent cessation 1–5 days ago suggests alcohol or sedative withdrawal and delirium tremens

key_questions.question: Has the patient been eating and drinking normally, or is there vomiting, diarrhea or poor intake?
key_questions.looking_for: Dehydration and electrolyte imbalance as reversible causes

key_questions.question: Does the patient have kidney failure, liver disease, diabetes, or other chronic illnesses?
key_questions.looking_for: Uremia, hepatic encephalopathy, hypoglycemia or hyperglycemia as triggers

key_questions.question: Has the patient had memory problems or trouble thinking before this episode?
key_questions.looking_for: Pre-existing dementia or mild cognitive impairment, which is the strongest risk factor and may coexist

key_questions.question: Has the patient had recent surgery, anesthesia, or been in the hospital or ICU?
key_questions.looking_for: Hospitalization, surgery and ICU stay as precipitants

key_questions.question: Is the patient seeing or hearing things that are not there, or acting suspicious or fearful?
key_questions.looking_for: Visual hallucinations and paranoid delusions, which support delirium over dementia

key_questions.question: Has the patient had a seizure, loss of consciousness, or stiff neck with headache?
key_questions.looking_for: Meningitis, encephalitis or nonconvulsive status epilepticus; these are life-threatening and must not be missed

key_questions.question: Does the patient wear glasses or hearing aids, and are they available?
key_questions.looking_for: Sensory impairment that worsens confusion and is easily corrected

accepted_names: Altered mental status due to delirium
reasoning_points: Acute onset over hours to days with a fluctuating course during the day, often worse at night
Inattention is the core deficit, with disorientation and disorganized thinking
Either hypoactive (withdrawn, sleepy) or hyperactive (agitated, hallucinating) presentation, or a mix of both
Evidence of an underlying trigger such as infection, dehydration, electrolyte disturbance, new or changed medication, alcohol or sedative withdrawal, surgery, pain or sleep deprivation
Pre-existing dementia or cognitive impairment is the strongest risk factor and may coexist with delirium
Bedside glucose checked immediately and reversible causes addressed before attributing symptoms to dementia or a psychiatric disorder
Structured bedside assessment such as the Confusion Assessment Method confirms the diagnosis
Red flags excluded: fever with neck stiffness, focal neurologic deficit, head trauma, hypoxia, hypotension or persistent unresponsiveness
Dementia, depression, primary psychosis, nonconvulsive status epilepticus, CNS infection, alcohol withdrawal, hepatic encephalopathy and hypoglycemia considered and distinguished

easy: Older hospitalized patient with sudden confusion and disorientation after admission
Clear fluctuation with worse confusion at night and clearer periods in the morning
Identifiable trigger such as urinary tract infection, new sedative or recent surgery
Hyperactive presentation with agitation and visual hallucinations
medium: Hypoactive delirium mistaken for depression, fatigue or dementia
Patient with known dementia who becomes more confused, requiring recognition of delirium superimposed on dementia
Multiple potential triggers present at once, such as infection plus electrolyte disturbance plus new medication
Older adult with a normal white count despite infection
Delirium as the only sign of sepsis or hypoxia
hard: Fluctuating confusion with no obvious cause, requiring broad workup including imaging and EEG
Persistent unresponsiveness that does not improve after correcting obvious causes, suggesting nonconvulsive status epilepticus
Alcohol or sedative withdrawal with autonomic overactivity and risk of seizures
Hepatic encephalopathy presenting with fluctuating confusion, sleep inversion and asterixis
Younger patient with delirium from drug intoxication or poisoning
Patient with focal deficit or head trauma requiring urgent imaging before lumbar puncture
